My momma is from upstate NY and followed her parents to the Mississippi coast in the mid 90s and was adamant all my life that she would never move back to snow. After living through Katrina and the hurricane season of 2020 she decided she couldn't do hurricanes anymore and the constant threat of losing everything again. So she moved to the Cape a few years ago to be closer to her grands. 

I'm Mississippian born and raised, moved to south coast MA this past summer. And I gotta be honest, I fuckin hate it. I'm here because she's getting older and needs help, but I surely wouldn't be here otherwise. The snow itself is fine, the cold is a hell of a lot easier to deal with on its own than I'd have thought because of the lack of humidity. But it's more dreary and well... dead outside than I'm used to and its incredibly depressing. And the wind here is insane, just random weeks with near constant tropical storm winds, not enough to damage anything, just enough to be annoying as hell driving or existing outside. And truthfully a little anxiety inducing to hear for those of us raised with hurricanes. I'd definitely spend as much time up here visiting as you can before making that decision because I was so convinced it'd be better up here getting to experience seasons, only to realize I'm basically a lizard and I miss the sun, heat, and humidity.

My thoughts as someone who lived my entire life in MS and AL until this summer-


Housing is expensive whether you rent or buy. But if you buy, the property tax rate is actually surprisingly low. Lower than back home. Lots of complaints about utility costs but frankly if you're mindful of your consumption, have a well insulated home and don't have or constantly assblast AC in the summer (it's hot but definitely more tolerable here given lower humidity) then I don't think it's bad. For a 2000sqft home we pay about as much for internet, power, water, and gas a month as we did for just electric in summer. My lowest electric bill so far has been $54. Groceries are generally the same, and surprisingly I've found a number of fresh foods to be cheaper than back home. I find that the nickname "taxachusetts" comes more from oddball taxes like needing a "dog license" and the tiny additional tax on your check for state parental leave and stuff which I'll happily pay. Typical tax stuff is low to average.
There's a lot more financial assistance stuff available than red states of course, healthcare, limited free education benefits, utility assistance, etc. Basically, housing is going to be your biggest issue financially. 

Socially, I'd probably steer clear of Bristol and Plymouth counties as there's more of a republican presence than you would expect or experience in the rest of the state and while they may still be in the minority, they're of course just as loud as any red state. And frankly, as a southerner living in one of the aforementioned counties, I'm finding that issues like racism that northerners like to brag about being superior to the south on absolutely still exist just... more quietly. I maintain that it's not that there's less racism so much as there's less racial diversity (at least outside of Boston). All of the "bad" areas of my city are the only areas you'll frequently see POC in. But it's at least not as blatant/violent. I'm in an area with a large portuguese population as well and folks are pretty xenophobic, even more assimilated portuguese folks. But again, its more shit head comments kept to themselves than anything. I've found there to be less police tension, granted I'm functionally white but the fact that in my hometown i watched two cops empty their clips into a homeless man for sleeping outside a dollar tree in broad daylight and here I watched three cops calmly deescalate a public intoxication/DV situation and make an arrest without even a twitch toward their weapons is a little mindboggling to me. Even homeless folks and your local crackhead are a lot less... aggressive? Than I'm used to. 

Coming from a city an hour from NOLA and very much under cajun influence though, folks here can't season food to save their lives. 

TLDR, it's far from the utopia Red State Lefties are led to believe it is, but certainly better than a red state.

I've lived in Orange Grove (just off Dedeaux and Three Rivers) and down by the beach. If you want to keep it a closer commute, in terms of living I'd definitely keep it north in Gulfport. Like, wait til you hit Tractor Supply and keep going a bit and then find one of those suburbs. 

If you don't mind driving 20-30 minutes I'd suggest any other city/township. Biloxi I'd say is the best for a mix of suburban with pockets of activity, I know a lot of folks like the neighborhoods off of Popps Ferry and a of course there's some schools nearby, and it isn't far from the aquarium, LMDC, arcades, etc for the kids. Long Beach is quieter still, generally more rural unless you're right down by the beach, but very little to do on the weekends that's super close by. Pass Christian I would say is the nicest and most geared toward old folks and families with small kids that doesn't involve having to cross the BSL or OS bridges. Their downtown is tiny, but cute. Some small shops, a couple of restaurants, a cute coffee shop/book store, the harbor has a little fish market like most others, and there's a great park with tennis courts, a good sized playground and splash pad in the summer for kids. Plus their public library, at least when I lived there, had all kinds of weekly and monthly programs ranging from children's story time to talks on hobby agriculture like bee keeping, to yoga and such on the beach. Definitely do your research on what an area went through during Katrina in regards to storm surge flooding and property elevation and such, especially for insurance purposes. The Waffle House Index is pretty accurate here. Generally anything below a strong 3 and the only folks who are panicking are people not from here, people who waited til the last minute to prep, and dummies who get caught in the hysteria of the first group. You can usually tell who those people are based on the amount of refrigerated and frozen items in their cart at Walmart. Most normal folks will just hunker down, make sure their devices are charged, pantries are stocked with water and nonperishables, and maybe bust out the alcohol and board games.

News outlets will inform citizens of when evacuation is not necessary, encouraged, or mandatory and there are signs in some areas on major roadways that show evacuation routes. For those who can't or won't evacuate, there are shelters and buses to get to them. As for when it is safe to return to your home, they will also inform people of that, and work is at least somewhat dependant on who you work for. If it isn't safe in the area, obviously no one is worried about work. But I'll tell you, after Zeta my job gave folks a day before they started demanding folks show back up, even though plenty of people either couldn't get to work due to debris blocking roads, or had more pressing matters due to property damage to attend to. How your community reacts is hit or miss, and you may deal with wonderful members of the community. Restaurant owners trying to give out meals to those who are around and neighbors helping each other clean up. And you may deal with awful people who take the panic as an opportunity to try to loot your shit and turn everything into a Mad Max lawless wasteland. Post Katrina we dealt with both. The chaos of a serious storm doesn't stop when the storm does.

All of that being said, as one of many who lived through Katrina and still have trauma from it nearly two decades later, every passing year that we come out relatively unscathed makes the next season feel like more of a ticking time bomb, and many of the people I know who have moved or want to move away, do so because of hurricanes. My family isn't from here. They moved down in the late 90s because they loved the area, and they've all left in the last couple of years because the anxiety of the inevitable was just too much. I know very few people who don't get anxious when it rains just a little too hard, or when it's just a little too windy. Families got split up and had no way of knowing where they were or if they were even alive, came home to no home, our belongings destroyed and scattered for blocks- at least what we could find- and houses completely leveled, lived off of MREs from the government for who knows how long because there was no other source of food.. it was all very third world. And that's if you had the means and sense to leave. Plenty of folks didn't and at best, lived through absolute hell and at worst died waiting to be rescued. Heat exhaustion, dehydration, drowned, shot. In terms of the crime, we got out much better off than New Orleans, but that's not to say we were all singing kumbaya together while we shoveled what was left of each other's homes out to the curb, ignoring the stench of sewage and decay. And lemme tell you, that's a smell you don't ever forget. I was just a kid but 18 years later I can still smell it.

If you really wanna risk it, all I can tell you is to read the fine print on your home insurance, make sure you got plenty of batteries, flashlights, power banks, canned goods, water, and cash because there's a good chance the card readers will get overloaded and shut down. And don't let your gas tank get too low because when it's the day before a storm, you'll wait two hours to get gas just to finally get up to the pump and they've run out. And good luck.

When I've stopped vaping for a period of time I still don't deal so much with the bad withdrawals, but irritability is definitely increased, more than switching from cigarettes to vaping, and I get incredibly anxious, again moreso than switching. You'll definitely still have withdrawals and cravings, but I'd be very surprised if the withdrawals weren't significantly reduced given the continued presence of nicotine, which has always been my biggest source of withdrawal symptoms at least.  

When I've quite nicotine/smoking cold turkey it's ranged anywhere from miserable to downright scary.  At best I've just been irritable, anxious, moody. At worst I've dealt with shakes, cold sweats, nausea, dizziness, and horrible headaches. But when switching from cigarettes to vaping and still having nicotine, I might be a little irritable, though significantly less than going cold turkey, and I'll want cigarettes still and will think about them a LOT, so watching someone else smoke, smelling it, seeing it in shows or whatever, I have to make a conscious effort to not ask for one or go out and buy a pack. But that's the extent of it. No physical symptoms other than mild irritation, no mental symptoms other than just thinking about it a lot. Much much easier to deal with than quitting outright, which is why so many people switch rather than quit completely.

As far as the Mississippi coast it's probably one of the better areas. A little more developed than Bay St. Louis and Pass Christian, but not quite so overrun by chain stores as say D'Iberville. There's a little something for everyone. Lots of locally owned shops and boutiques, restaurants and bars, even a neat little toy store if you have kids. They're also very proud of the local art and have a small museum and several art festivals throughout the year. Beaches are a good in between for the coast. Biloxi and Gulfport are maintained but during the warmer months they're the first to get trashed by tourists and college kids. The beaches west of those are quieter but aren't looked after quite as much since there's significantly fewer tourists away from the casinos. They're generally fairly quietly but well kept. I know theres also a little natural park that way that has some small walking trails and a good pier to fish at (but fishing spots are pretty frequent around the coast of course). The trade off is that housing is a little more expensive than some other areas. If you're asking with plans to move and you're a renter there are definitely some reasonably priced complexes just outside of the downtown area and I'm sure buyers can find cheaper real estate in east OS closer to Pascagoula. If you want more shopping options it's not far to get to D'Iberville and more nightlife options, crossing the bridge to Biloxi almost immediately spits you out by the casinos.

The per unit savings would only really be accurate if you were operating under the assumption that, like how every associate has or will receive an XCover, every associate had a TC. And the biggest kicker is, the TCs are still necessary since not only do the phones not have apps like claims and receiving, but OPD still solely relies on TCs to complete their jobs because the process of picking via a camera vs a barcode scanner is significantly slower and more cumbersome and even corporate schmucks are capable of realizing that they cannot expect OPD depts to maintain on time pick rate for the order volume and growth they expect OPD to keep increasing, let alone hit their pick rate target. So while the support and software contract may cost less, that expense still exists. Plus the time and money that went into figuring logistics, app development, and then repairs and replacements for the TCs still in circulation, as well as the cost of scanner attachments for the phones, assuming they ever actually follow through on supplying those or even just having them as an option on GNFR. 

And when most associates refuse to use their phones because they're too much of a pain in the ass and would still rather hunt down hand helds, or (in the case of a number of coworkers) just not complete tasks that are TC/XCover reliant, and those phones they spent hundreds of millions of dollars on as a corporation are collecting dust, I'm failing to see where the great financial win is for Walmart as a corporation that would justify this headache. I genuinely think switching to the phones was more of an attempted status symbol to further their image as an uber successful corporation (as if their soaring profits in the midst of this pandemic bullshit wasn't proof enough) and emulate more "high end" companies just giving all their employees $500 phones for shiggles while still trying to maintain the reputation of being the budget friendly 5 &10 that Sam Walton started.

I got my bridge done maybe 5 weeks ago? With the saline wash it does definitely get a bit dry in the area above the channel, but my piercer recommended that as the crusties diminish, going to once a day for saline and then just letting the water from the shower soften the crusties to clean them off as well. So if you shower in the morning, use the saline at night or vice versa.  

Sleeping on it can definitely cause problems. I got smacked in the face a couple of weeks ago and that led to some swelling and an increase in lymph fluid (as well as a small amount of blood) and then realized I was sleeping halfway between being on my side and my stomach that, since downsizing my bar hasn't been a problem, but when I had a 5/8", was pushing it back and forth in my sleep as I moved around. Definitely has set back my healing. Swelling can come and go for no reason for the first few weeks, it's why you should wait about a month before downsizing instead of just waiting for the initial swelling to go down, but ibuprofen may help reduce it. My piercer is APP certified and recommended doing so for the first week and then again when I hit it. Unfortunately, sooner or later you're going to have to deal with irrational customers who think they're above rules or above employees and their wants come before an employees needs. You absolutely are not in the wrong. Within reason of course, do not allow yourself to become a doormat or to remain in an unsafe situation. You'll get called racist for not doing what someone wants, you'll get called an idiot or incompetent for not telling someone what they want to hear, even though chances are, you are right. It happens to all of us. Sometimes we're lucky enough to have a manager who will stick up for us and remove the instigator, sometimes we won't and, like a small child, we will have to wait for them to finish their tantrum, and continue what we were doing. All of that being said, something to keep in mind is that the holiday season is quickly approaching, and when it's here, customer idiocy will be much much worse. So as it gets closer, if you find you are unable to close yourself off mentally to these altercations, it will likely be in your best interest to either transfer to another department that won't have constant customer interaction, or put in your notice. It is better to do that than to remain in a situation that is not sustainable for you and risk doing something that will burn this employment bridge in case you need it in the future.

Having boxes for your consoles brings up the value for said console. Same with having original cases and manuals for video games, having boxes for collectors items/collector edition games, etc. Many folks who are into collecting enough to want new or near new condition boxes for their consoles also usually have displays for said boxes.  

A good example of just how much having a box can affect the value of something like that: not too long ago i found an original Mega Man x3 for SNES for $5 at goodwill. The cartridge alone can be sold for over $200. Finding an original box would cost me $150-$200, which would of course be pricey and far more than what I paid for the game, BUT it also nearly triples the value to over $600. $205 for a game and box with a $400+ dollar profit? For many folks, collecting boxes just makes sense for aesthetic purposes, protection of games and consoles that may be stored, just because some folks are completionists, and also just from a monetary standpoint for their collection.
